section.title: Getting to Staff Engineer at Big Tech: A Five-Person Panel on Scope, Relationships, and Promotion
section.deck: Five engineers who reached staff level at Meta, Google, Activision, Netflix and Airbnb discuss the projects behind their promotions, how to find scope, and why relationships and communication matter as much as technical depth.

blocks.text: Rahul hosts four engineers (Lee, Ryan Peterman, Carly and Zach) and also answers as a panelist. Between them they have worked at staff level, or the equivalent, at Meta, Google, Activision, Netflix and Airbnb. Their shared view is that staff level changes the kind of work, not only its size. A staff engineer is expected to influence other people, to find problems that are worth the company's time, and to be known well enough that others can vouch for the result. They disagree on details, such as how much a staff engineer should still code, but they return again and again to three points: relationships, clear communication, and a direct read of the company's own promotion process. Everything below is the speakers' own experience and opinion, not company policy.
blocks.heading: The panel's view: staff scope is found through problems and people, not through code alone

blocks.title: Levels discussed, as summarized by the host from a levels.fyi diagram
rows: No staff title; the level after senior is principal

blocks.title: Panelists and the background each one stated
headers: Background as stated in the panel
rows: In software engineering since 2004. At Amazon from 2012, first as an SDE II and later in people management. Then a staff-level IC role at Meta, which Lee says did not go well. About a year and a half before the panel, moved to Google as a staff engineer (chat, then Gmail notifications).
Staff engineer at Meta, working on Instagram. Graduated in 2017, spent about eight months at an Amazon satellite office, then joined Meta as a new graduate. Three promotions in about five years.

At Activision. A senior manager who also holds an IC title equivalent to staff (lead engineer). Finished graduate school in 2017, started as a junior data scientist, joined Activision at senior level and took about two years to reach lead. Works in security.

Began in data engineering at Facebook in 2016. Then Netflix, where every engineer held the senior title. Then Airbnb, where Zach received the official staff title and stayed two years. Left about six months before the panel to create content full time.

Runs Taro. About four and a half years at Meta, going from senior to staff. About two and a half years at Pinterest, where Rahul was rejected for promotion twice. Before that, a startup that Pinterest acquired.

blocks.label: Pace: promotion is not a race (Lee and Rahul)
blocks.text: Rahul says being rejected for promotion twice at Pinterest gave Rahul both the manager's and the candidate's view of the process. Lee says Lee failed three attempts at the senior SDE III level at Amazon, and also failed the first try to reach L6 as a manager. Lee reached the staff-equivalent level roughly 16 or 17 years into a career. Lee's point is that several panelists rose very quickly, by changing companies or succeeding fast inside one, but that is not the only path and a missed first senior promotion is not unusual.

blocks.question: What project or projects got each panelist to staff level?
answer: Zach moved up by changing companies. At Netflix every engineer held the senior title, but Zach felt the responsibilities were already staff-level, and Airbnb later hired Zach at staff. The project Zach credits is an asset inventory at Netflix. Netflix used microservices, which give each team ownership but also leave thousands of separate applications that could each hold their own vulnerabilities. Zach built a graph database describing applications, code bases, data sets and employees and how they connect to one another. The work took about two years.

Lee was also hired at staff level rather than promoted into it. Lee had managed people for about three years at Amazon before joining Meta. Lee says technical work alone was not enough. Some people point to a large, complex project they delivered alone, but staff-level readiness also depends on whether they planned the work, split it into parallel work streams, and reduced risk so the hardest part was not left until last. Lee's hardest technical project was a custom class loader that let an Android app use multiple executable files before Google supported that, so that Amazon's video app (now Prime Video) and its combined apps did not hit the method limit. Lee did not want engineers forced to write poor code to fit a technical limit.

Ryan Peterman describes a large efficiency project that made video processing at Instagram much cheaper, 94 percent cheaper for some basic encodings. Ryan says the project reached staff level because Ryan created the scope: Ryan found the problem, convinced people it was worth doing, got buy-in, and led execution. Ryan stepped in personally only on the riskiest components. Several engineers did most of the work while Ryan led and reviewed code. Ryan stresses that staff is one of the first levels where influencing others is a baseline expectation, because software is collaborative.

Carly says the step up is not just technical brilliance. It comes down to trust and to being a collaborator that others rely on. Carly points to a presentation of security findings to an executive leader and the CTO. Carly could explain technical work to people who did not want to sit in an engineering meeting, and received a job offer from a leader in that meeting. That became an internal move to staff. Carly says this is not a normal route. The wider lesson is to know your numbers, be ready to state your impact to technical and non-technical audiences, and work on large, cross-business problems that address a real pain point. The people who decide on promotion are often both kinds of audience.

Rahul names two projects at Meta. One was an internal tool that improved debugging of the product. Rahul measured that it saved thousands of engineering hours in a year, and other engineers could plug in their own debugging tools, which multiplied the impact. The other was re-architecting the product's calling architecture, moving it onto another team's set of APIs. Rahul's lesson is to think in terms of a portfolio of bets. A big-tech company has many things outside your control, so pair one main project with a smaller one you control, and switch when one is blocked. Two or three projects is realistic, not ten. Rahul adds that a company must also have enough business need for staff-level scope, so some people get promoted simply by moving to a company that needs their skills.

followups.question: Is a staff promotion usually a sudden result of one project?
answer: One panelist says no. A promotion packet is normally a track record covering several half-year review periods. By the time it reaches the promotion committee, people should already know the candidate's name and the candidate should have been doing near-staff or staff-level work for some time.

followups.question: What kind of impact makes people notice a staff engineer?
answer: Zach describes two directions of impact. Vertical impact is the direct effect on the business. Horizontal impact is helping a team move faster by improving how work gets done, not only what is built. Zach's Netflix example was a Groovy script that removed unused dependencies from the deployable file for pipelines. Zach estimates each deploy saved one to seven minutes, which at five or six deploys a day is about 30 minutes to an hour a day per engineer. Zach says the rest is adoption rather than technical excellence.

Another panelist adds a rough calculation: a 16 percent speedup across 66 people is the equivalent of a 10x engineer. The same panelist says that the very senior engineers they studied, three levels above staff, often make compounding improvements to tooling used by thousands of engineers.

blocks.question: How should a senior or staff engineer balance delegating work and doing it personally? (An attendee, Brian, asked, and Rahul rephrased the question.)
answer: Zach recalls weekly conversations with an Airbnb manager about whether Zach was managing, delegating and coding enough. Zach loves to code Scala all day, and says that doing so has sometimes been to the team's detriment. Frank talks with a manager about how time is spent helped Zach see when more leadership was needed.

Lee says each person should know their own bias. An engineer who came from management may spend too much time on people and too little on reducing technical risk, while others lean the other way. The split does not need to be 50/50 each week. Lee also asks whether the engineer is leading from the front, finding the path and sending others down it, or from behind, pointing people in a direction. The answer varies by team: a team of peers differs from a team of new graduates. Lee says a manager's input helps here. A manager can point out that a 4 percent performance gain is good, but that no one knows which tools were used and nothing would be committed if the person were unavailable. In Lee's view how you do the work matters as much as what you do, and pairing with junior engineers helps them follow the threads.

Carly gives a manager's view, using Zach as an example. Carly would rather Zach had input into research, design and the roadmap of the big projects, so that someone with Zach's depth can quickly say what will break, and others do the deep implementation. Zach would step in when something is very complicated. Carly says the balance is hard to get right and is something to settle in talks with the manager.

Lee builds on this: one of the most powerful tools is asking the right question at the right time. A senior person who hears a team plan to re-architect something can say it is not the right focus and that it can sit behind a shim for now. Twenty minutes of that person's time can save two or three developer-years. Lee says that people's time should go where a design matters, because a missed hallway conversation can be costly.

followups.question: How should a staff engineer decide what not to work on?
answer: Zach tells of starting at Airbnb, when stakeholders were loud about certifying profitability numbers. As a newcomer Zach leaned on their requests. After about six months, Zach asked what difference certification would actually make, and the answer was essentially none, with roughly a one-day delay at most. Zach told the manager it was a case of diminishing returns, because the pipeline was too complicated to finish and the effort should move to higher-impact work. Another panelist notes that four people working on it for about four months likely cost the company a million dollars or more in salary alone, before counting what else they could have done.

A panelist adds that staff engineers must persuade, not just execute. Managers lean on staff engineers to identify what should and should not be worked on, which takes courage to tell stakeholders their project is being deprioritized. Explaining the reasoning is what keeps cross-functional partners' respect. Without it, the panelist says, mistrust builds first and resentment follows, and team dynamics can fall apart.

followups.question: Is a staff engineer always less hands-on?
answer: A panelist says no. It depends on the project and on the person's strengths. On a project with many senior people, staff may lead. Some very productive specialists, or people whose execution is worth four or five engineers, can have staff-level impact by doing most of the execution themselves. They are still expected to scale by sharing their knowledge. The panelist says not every staff engineer fits the tech-lead type: some are heads-down coders and some are domain specialists. Another panelist recalls that Meta had a "code machine" archetype for this kind of person.

blocks.question: Where does a staff engineer find, or make up, the scope?
answer: Lee says that as you become better than your managers at your job, they can no longer see the landmines or the technical constraints on a project. Lee rejects the idea of making up scope to justify a promotion as a bad choice. The job is to identify what is hurting the team and holding it back, raise it, and convince others to fix it. Lee compares this to the question of whether calculus was invented or discovered. Lee says most scope is discovered: work that others fear, do not see, or do not think is valuable, and that you must persuade them will speed up the next three projects or enable something the product could not do before. It may be found by looking through code, or in product requirements where there is a gap.

Lee's own habit is to put a hand up when no one else will. Lee gives the example of an old, fragile system that no one wants to touch. Lee says that when someone suggests turning it off, it may turn out to generate hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue, so it is worth a gradual replacement such as the strangler fig pattern. Lee admits that this sometimes leaves a person stuck with something awful.

Rahul sums up that asking how to find scope to justify a promotion is already the wrong question. The right one is what the most burning problems are, and what is on the mind of the manager, director and other engineers, and whether you can build something that helps them. Rahul compares it to a startup: you start with the problem, not a solution. Knowing those problems takes relationship building and being embedded in the organization.

blocks.question: How deliberate were you about building relationships with mentees, tech leads, managers and directors who might speak for you at review time? (Rahul)
answer: Carly calls it extremely intentional. Carly looks for people with a common problem or approach and teams up with them. Carly now has friends across business units, including people Carly seldom works with. Carly says that being remote full time makes this much harder than working in an office. Carly describes being an introverted extrovert and says people have to push against the urge not to message others, because no one will argue for you if no one knows you. Carly adds that someone working late and shown as online will not be noticed for that. People vouch for those they have seen deliver on time, on scope and on budget, and waiting to be rescued is the wrong approach.

Another panelist says that they were poor at happy hours, but their work was highly visible and they were promoted even during the pandemic. The key for them was to communicate the work: share the plan, get buy-in, and report the results. Writing and communication are strong tools, because in practice work does not market itself. A manager can be a cheerleader for only so long.

Lee says that being known was the difference between being stuck at L5 and being the person who pulled together Android engineers across Amazon, with data on when apps would run out of methods. People then send others to that person, and the person can point to the next step even when they lack the answer. Lee says human relationships are all there is. Lee worked remotely at Meta, never visited, and did not succeed. Lee had decent relationships but not the visibility, and so lacked help once things went wrong. Lee began asking one off-topic question a day on an Amazon team during the pandemic. Lee now does so in the chat rooms of two organizations at Google, and says people recognize Lee as the question person, which makes it easy to ask a product manager for help. Lee also suggests asking a manager whether anyone on the team needs a mentor, since even a no changes how they think of you, and sitting in on a product managers' event to understand their process and offer a developer's view. Lee says it may sound like politics, and sometimes it is, but it is part of the job. Lee, who describes being autistic with many social challenges, says Lee still has to do this to succeed.
Rahul offers a litmus test. If you asked a teammate what a person is known for, would they answer cohesively, such as saying that person is the expert on a system? If not, that is a bad sign.

followups.question: Is telling people about your work just self-promotion? (Sean, an attendee, asked what happened to modesty.)
answer: Rahul says do not frame it as bragging. Frame it as telling teammates how the work benefits them. Rahul's debugging tool at Meta made it faster to debug issues, and Rahul pitched it as a way to ease the work, help the product, and even help their performance reviews. Rahul's reframing is to give a call to action: here is how you can get plugged in.

Other panelists agree that sharing knowledge is mutual. Explaining what you tried, what failed and what worked, or building a lower-level framework others can reuse, makes the work more useful and spares others from learning the hard way. A panelist notes that big-tech engineers are often curious and open, and so they want to hear it. Lunch-and-learns and demos, such as a short screen share of a browser extension, can change how others work. The panelists draw the line between bragging and teaching there.

blocks.question: What heuristics improve the chance of promotion to staff, for example the choice of team, its size, or infrastructure versus product work? (Rahul)
answer: One panelist advises talking to someone above staff, such as a senior staff or principal engineer, asking what they would fix if they had the time, and doing that. A principal who supports your document goes a long way. The same panelist says to write the promotion document now, not when it feels ready. Show it to the people who review promotions and ask why they would reject it, then work on those gaps. Otherwise a promotion project might turn out not to be the right one, and that is the candidate's own fault. If the feedback is that you have never led anyone, the next project needs to show leadership rather than more code. Not understanding the process, the panelist says, leaves the outcome to luck.
Another panelist says they favor work on churn and finance-related problems at each company, because that is where the pain in the business is.

Zach puts the relationship with your manager first: without it, even a star will struggle. For data engineers, Zach says the data sets must be ones many other pipelines read from, such as master data. A data set made only for a visualization is not staff-level. A staff analytics engineer may instead own the whole chain from logging to data set to visualization and perhaps a model.

Another panelist describes three common rubric dimensions. One is the size of the work stream, such as the number of engineers and the duration. A second is complexity: could someone a level below solve it, or does it need domain knowledge such as distributed systems or AI? The third is impact: does it span several teams or reach significant business goals? This panelist says leverage comes from building things that other engineers build on, which biases toward infrastructure and tooling teams. Leading a very large product initiative is limited to a few places, and someone must grant permission, so those chances are fewer and harder to compete for.

followups.question: Is the preference for infrastructure a fair measure of staff-level work?
answer: Lee calls the focus on infrastructure and backend a legacy bias. Companies understood what top-level work on backend systems for billions of users looks like, but not what a principal front-end engineer does. Lee says people were advised to switch to a backend team to get promoted, which Lee considers wrong, though it has been real.
Zach adds that data engineering was new in 2016, and Facebook had only one staff data engineer at the time and now has dozens.

Rahul says the bias is not strictly front end versus back end. Engineers who build client-side infrastructure, such as an Android build system or a framework for client and server requests, also count. The key is that other engineers use what you build, and that is usually one layer below the people building the user-facing product.

blocks.question: Audience question: once you are at staff level, how do you keep exceeding expectations?
answer: One panelist says behaviors at staff and above are similar: influencing through others, growing people around you, and taking on the largest problems. What changes is that the initiatives are a step bigger. To exceed, find something larger in scope, such as influencing two larger organizations instead of one group of about 50, or building infrastructure for hundreds of engineers instead of dozens.

Zach, who says they received an exceeds rating at staff level at Airbnb for 2020, describes two parts. One was delivering the main "big rock" project, which for Zach was refining pricing and availability metrics. The other was design work on longer-term questions, such as a document on best practices for moving data from the data lake back into the Airbnb app, with feedback from principal engineers on edge cases. Zach says that missing the first means not meeting expectations at all, and doing both is what moves a person toward the senior staff level.

blocks.question: Audience question (Alan): what resources help with technical communication and finding mentorship?
answer: Rahul says the core skill is knowing your audience. At Meta, Rahul checked who belonged to an internal Workplace group before posting an update: engineers, leadership, or a cross-functional mix. Rahul then adjusted the depth, avoiding both too much detail and too little. Before a stand-up or meeting, find out who will be there and how much they know and care. Rahul has no book or video to suggest, and says the way to build empathy for different audiences is relationship building, which gives a sense of the personas you address.
Zach adds that posting on LinkedIn almost every day while at Airbnb taught Zach to say dense information concisely, because the platform rewards short posts. Zach recommends that skill for growth.

blocks.question: Audience question (sesh): should a senior engineer become a tech lead first on the way to staff?
answer: Ryan Peterman sees tech lead as a set of behaviors that can occur at any level, not as a level between senior and staff. Senior engineers on some teams lead smaller projects. Ryan suggests checking the company's own leveling system.

Another panelist cautions that if the missing pieces are leadership and visibility, being a tech lead may give more chances to practice them. But it is not necessarily a stepping stone, and doing the behaviors well does not guarantee a path to staff. A further panelist says the expected behaviors at each level should be written down at the company. Use that with your manager to see where you exceed and where you fall short, and ask for the documentation if you do not have it, because otherwise you can only guess.

blocks.question: Audience question (Sam): how can a data engineer show backend work to a manager who is not their day-to-day lead?
answer: Zach says that if there is no shiny front-end piece, part of the answer is to work with the data scientist or analyst who builds the visualization on top of your data. The other part is to show downstream impact. Zach says a data set can be sold as improving one of three kinds of decision: an executive's strategic decision, a data scientist's or analyst's product decision, or a machine-learning algorithm's automated decision. Zach's pricing and availability data sets at Airbnb fed Smart Pricing, an algorithm that sets prices for listings, which had a large effect on the business.

Zach adds that data engineers can also cite optimization numbers, such as a pipeline running 30 or 40 percent faster. At Airbnb, Zach cut the size of the pricing and availability data sets by 90 percent, so the company could use data 10 times smaller. Zach admits that data engineering can fall into the shadows because it lacks the show-it-off quality of a front end or a SQL query. Where the gain is only visibility, Zach suggests building a story around it.

blocks.label: Rahul's closing takeaway
blocks.text: Rahul's view is that the vast majority of engineers aiming for staff or senior roles, which Rahul puts at 99 percent, lack the skills of relationship building and talking to people. In Rahul's opinion, the task is less about the code than about working out what the problems are, who is hitting them, and how to solve them. The figure is Rahul's own estimate.
